cooling_items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized cooling system. Cooling within individual suites is provided by a combination of window-mounted air conditioners and portable indoor air-conditioning units.

These decentralized cooling devices are generally less efficient than modern centralized or heat-pump-based systems. Typical window and portable air-conditioning units operate with relatively low coefficients of performance (COP), often below 3.0, compared to high-efficiency heat pump systems which can achieve COP values exceeding 4.5–5.0 under favorable conditions.

In addition to reduced cooling efficiency, window-mounted air-conditioning units can negatively impact building envelope performance. Improper sealing around window installations may allow uncontrolled air infiltration during the heating season, increasing heat loss, draft complaints, and overall space-heating energy consumption. Installation of a air source heat pump (ASHP) system could be considered in a short term to mid term.
cooling_items.title: Window A/C Units

measures.existing_conditions: The building currently operates with two (2) gas-fired make-up air (MUA) units serving the corridor ventilation system. Each unit provides approximately 10,000 CFM of supply air and includes an integral natural gas burner rated at approximately 270 MBH. The units operate independently and rely on direct gas combustion for space heating, with limited centralized temperature control or scheduling. This results in reduced part-load efficiency, limited system coordination, and increased natural gas consumption during the heating season.
measures.measure_title: Aging MUA Hydronic Conversion with BAS and VFDs
measures.notes: Replace two aging gas-fired MUA units with new hydronic VFD MUA units served by a dedicated 97.1% efficient Fulton EXE-1500 condensing boiler and BAS controls. This measure is intended to reduce natural gas consumption, improve ventilation scheduling and turndown performance, and provide better system-level control of corridor heating and ventilation.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the two (2) existing gas-fired MUA units with two (2) new hydronic MUA units equipped with variable frequency drive (VFD) supply fans and hot water heating coils, each rated at approximately 9,000 CFM. Heating for the new MUA system will be provided by one (1) dedicated Fulton EXE-1500 high-efficiency condensing boiler (1,500 MBH, 97.1% efficiency), including new pumps, glycol system, and associated hydronic piping.

The new MUA units will be integrated with the building automation system (BAS) to enable centralized monitoring and control. The system will operate based on a scheduled ventilation strategy with fan speeds set at approximately 50% from 11:00 PM to 6:00 AM, 90% from 6:00 AM to 9:00 AM, 70% from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, and 90% from 5:00 PM to 11:00 PM. The units will maintain a discharge air temperature of approximately 65°F, with a warm weather shutdown at 55°F outdoor air temperature.

The boiler will operate under an outdoor air temperature reset schedule, ranging from approximately 90°F supply at 60°F outdoor air temperature to 140°F supply at -5°F outdoor air temperature. BAS integration will include monitoring and control of fan speed, unit status, discharge air temperature, glycol temperature, and outdoor air temperature.

This retrofit will eliminate direct-fired ventilation heating, improve part-load efficiency through condensing operation, and enable optimized ventilation control through scheduling and modulation.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is currently served by a heating-only hydronic distribution system. Space heating is provided through copper-fin baseboard heaters and hydronic radiators supplied by a centralized boiler plant located in the main mechanical room.

The building does not have a central cooling system. No in-suite fan coil units, chillers, or centralized cooling infrastructure are present. As a result, suite-level cooling, where provided, relies on window A/C or portable air-conditioning units. These localized cooling devices typically operate independently, are relatively inefficient, and contribute to increased electrical demand during the cooling season.
measures.measure_title: Convert Baseboard Heater to Mini-Split Heat Pump Systems
measures.notes: Replace current system with air-source heat pumps, allowing simultaneous heating and cooling.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing hydronic baseboard heating systems with mini-split air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems to provide both space heating and cooling at the suite level.

The existing hydronic baseboard system relies on centrally generated hot water distributed throughout the building. While functional for heating, this system provides heating only, operates at relatively high distribution temperatures, and does not provide cooling. In addition, system efficiency is constrained by boiler plant performance, distribution losses, and limited zone-level control.

In contrast, mini-split heat pump systems typically operate at a COP of approximately 3 to 4 under suitable operating conditions, allowing them to deliver three to four units of heat for each unit of electrical energy consumed by transferring heat from the outdoor air to the indoor space. This results in a substantial reduction in energy consumption while maintaining or improving occupant comfort.

In addition to improved heating efficiency, the proposed mini-split systems would introduce dedicated cooling capability to the suites. This would eliminate the need for separate window-mounted or portable air-conditioning units, improving overall system efficiency, reducing peak electrical demand, and simplifying long-term maintenance.

The proposed upgrade would transition the building from an aging, single-function heating system to a modern, high-efficiency heating and cooling solution, improving occupant comfort, operational performance, and long-term energy efficiency.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

misc_items.text: The building envelope appears to be in generally good condition, with no significant signs of air leakage or deterioration observed at the time of the site visit. Envelope components appear to be performing as intended.
misc_items.title: Envelope Condition (Good)

misc_items.text: In aging buildings, even double-pane window assemblies may experience gradual deterioration of glazing seals over time. Loss of insulating gas or degradation of the sealed air space between panes can reduce overall thermal performance. While the existing windows were observed to be in generally fair condition, it would be prudent to incorporate sealant renewal and eventual glazing upgrades into the building’s long-term capital planning strategy.
misc_items.title: Window condition (Aging double pane)

misc_items.text: Lighting throughout the building is generally in good working order. Common areas, corridors, and service spaces appear to be equipped with a mix of LED and fluorescent fixtures. No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.
misc_items.title: Lighting condition and controls

ventilation_items.text: Ventilation for the building is provided by two (2) make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas.
ventilation_items.title: Rooftop MUA

ventilation_items.text:
The existing make-up air (MUA) unit is equipped with a constant-speed supply fan and an integral gas-fired heating burner, providing heating-only capacity. The unit does not include variable frequency drive (VFD) control and does not provide mechanical cooling.

The absence of VFD control results in fixed airflow operation regardless of actual ventilation demand, limiting part-load efficiency and increasing electrical energy consumption. The gas-fired heating section provides basic winter heating capability; however, without cooling capacity, heat recovery, or advanced modulation control, the system offers limited seasonal optimization and indoor temperature regulation.

At the time of the site visit, the unit was observed to be in functional condition with no visible mechanical deficiencies. However, the configuration reflects an older, conventional ventilation design with limited energy efficiency and control flexibility.
ventilation_items.title: No VFD + Gas Fire (heating only)

ventilation_items.text: Supply-air temperatures and airflow patterns were observed to be consistent with normal operation. The gas-fired heating burner was reported by building staff to have been replaced recently. While the MUA units remain operational, the equipment appears to be approaching the latter portion of its service life. Replacement or upgrade to a high-efficiency MUA unit may be considered in the near term.
ventilation_items.title: Aging but funtional MUA
